panels.attribution_text: Olusanya and Baiyeroju. Emergency management: ophthalmia neonatorum.. Community eye health 2018. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
in_text_mentions: Gonococcal ON is less common than chlamydial conjunctivitis but is more severe,1 so parents are more likely to bring their babies to hospital. It becomes noticeable 2–5 days after birth with copious purulent eye discharge (Figure 1) and severe redness and swelling of the conjunctiva. The eyelids are often very swollen. If untreated, or inadequately treated, it can very quickly result in corneal haziness and perforation, causing blindness. Babies with very severe disease may have systemic complications such as septicaemia and meningitis.

in_text_mentions: st polyclinic follow-ups. However, the case was referred to an ophthalmologist only after the third visit to the polyclinic when the condition worsened. Upon receiving the referral, the ophthalmology team noticed that she was irritable during examination of her left eye. Ophthalmic examination of the left eye revealed an erythematous swollen eyelid with minimal yellowish discharge (Figure 1a). Pseudomembranes and associated meibomitis were noted (Figure 1b). The conjunctiva was severely injected and chemotic with subconjunctival haemorrhage. Furthermore, there was ophthalmoplegia at all gazes.

panels.rationale: Single ophthalmic clinical photograph of a 12-day-old infant with neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis caused by fluoroquinolone-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, i.e., ophthalmia neonatorum. Caption and in-text confirm bilateral conjunctival injection, pronounced left eyelid edema, periorbital erythema, and left conjunctival hemorrhage; the image shows the left eye with marked conjunctival hyperemia/chemosis and lid edema. Real human-patient image, no third-party copyright, classic untreated presentation. [raw subtype: gonococcal]
panels.attribution_text: Mizushima et al. Neonatal Gonococcal Conjunctivitis Caused by Fluoroquinolone-Resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae.. Emerging infectious diseases 2025. doi:10.3201/eid3110.250895. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure Figure.
panels.figure_caption: Bilateral conjunctival infection, pronounced left eyelid edema, and periorbital erythema observed in a 12-day-old infant in case of neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis caused by fluoroquinolone-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Japan, 2023.
in_text_mentions: At admission, we recorded vital signs, laboratory test results, and urine test results (Appendix). Physical examination revealed bilateral conjunctival injection, pronounced left eyelid edema, and periorbital erythema (Figure). The corneas were clear, having no evidence of epithelial defect, ulceration, or perforation. We noted no anterior chamber abnormalities, and ocular motility was preserved. We observed a conjunctival hemorrhage in the left eye.
